newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian masses live in poverty.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian masses live in poverty.

text.p: No water. No telephone. Nights without electricity.

That describes the conditions of the 74 captives held by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, where utilities were cut off early in the three-week siege. It is also true for the people of the Villa Emilia shantytown 15 miles (25 km) to the north.

"We're just like them. The difference is that when the hostages come out they'll go back to their big houses and we'll still be here," Rosa Salvador, 45, said, gesturing at the dilapidated shack that houses her family of six.
Below her, the dusty shantytown stretched for miles. Rows of dull brown dwellings blended into the dry dunes along Peru's central Pacific coast. There were no roads.
Villa Emilia is one of hundreds of makeshift settlements surrounding the capital that have sprouted seemingly overnight and serve as home to half of the Lima area's 6 million people.

The box-like homes are made from makeshift materials -- cardboard, wood, plastic sheeting and matting made from reeds. Salvador and her family are among the roughly 13 million of Peru's 24 million people who live in poverty.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas who seized the Japanese residence in a spectacular Dec. 17 assault say they represent people like the Salvadors -- a claim strongly disputed by President Alberto Fujimori's government.
In a tough speech on Thursday, the Peruvian leader called the MRTA "terrorists" bent on pointless destruction that only aggravated the misery of Peru's poor.
But Salvador's 19-year-old son Omar said: "The MRTA are portrayed as the baddies of the film, but it's true what they say. Some people here don't eat all day."

"We hardly ever eat meat. I cannot remember the last time," his mother said. But she said the rebels had few supporters among the people of Villa Emilia. "It's true that there's a lot of poverty, but that (taking hostages) isn't the way to show it."
The Salvador family's main income comes from Rosa's husband, Arturo, who works as a builder and decorator. On a good day he earns $7.50. Usually it is less and often it is nothing.
His wife makes a little extra selling ice cream from home. "We all work, even my 13-year-old son. They go to clean houses, sell clothes, anything," she said.

The tiny shack where they live has no floor so the family shuffles barefoot in the sand on which the shantytown is built. In the main room a large rusting refrigerator stands in one corner, dominating a room filled by two wooden chairs, a bench and an old sofa without cushions.
The reed-matting roof is full of holes, and there is no bathroom. "We have to go outside, everybody does," Salvador said. Residents dig holes in the sandy earth and periodically cover them over.
Water is delivered irregularly by a truck. "It should come every day but sometimes it doesn't stop and we're without water for two or three days," she said.

While condemning the MRTA's methods, she hoped their action would force authorities to take notice of the conditions under which poor Peruvians live. "The ministers with their big salaries don't understand. I wish they'd come here and see how we live."
